title: The Farmer's Broken Back
subtitle: A Thematic and Sonic Architecture of Agrarian Collapse
genre: Delta Blues / Heavy Folk / Heartland Rock

acts.title: The Golden Age & The Trap
acts.subtitle: The Boom
acts.description: The manic energy of the early 1970s agricultural expansion, Earl Butz's 'Get Big or Get Out' philosophy, heavy debt leverage, and the 1980s trap snapping shut as Volcker interest rates spike to 21.5%.

acts.title: The Industrial Machine
acts.subtitle: The Squeeze
acts.description: The structural forces of multinational corporate consolidation: the 'Big Four' meatpacking oligopoly, the shrinking 14-cent farmer share of the food dollar, and the geopolitical trade war silo gluts.

acts.title: The Feudalism of Feathers
acts.subtitle: The Loss of Agency
acts.description: The total surrender of operational and biological autonomy: the zero-sum poultry tournament system, patented terminator seeds and annual technology fees, and Code 502 tractor software lockouts.

acts.title: The Human Cost
acts.subtitle: The Fracture
acts.description: The psychological and communal fracture: Dicamba drift turning neighboring farms into hostile battlegrounds, the humiliation of the foreclosure auctioneer's dirge, and hollowed-out empty main streets.

acts.title: The Renewal
acts.subtitle: Remediation & Future
acts.description: The arduous crossing from industrial addiction to soil regeneration: braving the financial 'valley of death', reviving Sherman Act antitrust enforcement, and standing upright with an enduring spirit.

tracks.title: Fencerow to Fencerow (The Earl's Command)
tracks.tagline: The Earl's Command & The Illusion of Infinite Boom
tracks.vocal_profile: Fast, driving Heartland Country baritone with manic 70s optimism
tracks.theory: In 1973, USDA Secretary Earl Butz dismantled the New Deal supply management system, ordering farmers to plant 'fencerow to fencerow' to feed the Soviet Union and global commodity markets. Guaranteed land appreciation and bank cheerleading sparked massive, unsustainable capital overexpansion.
tracks.summary: The opening movement of the cycle. A Midwestern grain farmer aggressively tears down windbreaks, fills in wetlands, and borrows against paper equity, intoxicated by the intoxicating promise of infinite growth before the trap snaps shut.
tracks.clean_lyrics:
The man from Washington stood on the tailgate
With a shiny suit and a smile just like a shark
He pointed at the oaks along the creek bed
He said "Boys you're living in the dark"
He said "The Russians need the wheat and we need dollars"
He said "Scarcity is just a sinful doubt"
He loosened up his tie and popped his collar
He screamed "You gotta get big or get out!"

Tear the treelines down!
Fill the ditches in!
Every inch of dirt is a way to win!
Plant it fencerow to fencerow!
Let the diesel engines scream and blow!
No room for weeds, no room for doubt
You gotta get big!
(Or get out!)

Granddad put those cedars in the thirties
To stop the wind from stealing all the soil
But Granddad didn't know about the future
And Granddad didn't burn this much oil
I hooked the chain up to the ancient maple
I felt the tractor buck and start to whine
We're feeding all the world, that is the staple
And profit is the only holy line!

Tear the treelines down!
Fill the ditches in!
Every inch of dirt is a way to win!
Plant it fencerow to fencerow!
Let the diesel engines scream and blow!
No room for weeds, no room for doubt
You gotta get big!
(Or get out!)

Ammonia tanks are hissing in the sun
The bank is open and the ink will run
Sign the paper, buy the big machine
Paint the whole world John Deere Green
Paint it green!
Paint it green!

Tear the treelines down!
Fill the ditches in!
Every inch of dirt is a way to win!
Plant it fencerow to fencerow!
Let the diesel engines scream and blow!
No room for weeds, no room for doubt
You gotta get big!
(Or get out!)

Fencerow to fencerow...
Plant it all...
Get big...

tracks.title: Leverage (The Gambler's Soil)
tracks.tagline: Paper Equity & The Allure of Debt
tracks.vocal_profile: Weary storytelling baritone over steady fingerpicked acoustic groove
tracks.theory: Agricultural debt expanded by over 300% during the 1970s. Commercial banks and the Farm Credit System extended massive loans secured only against rapidly inflating land values, transforming family farms into leveraged debt instruments vulnerable to any sudden macro shock.
tracks.summary: Sitting in a wood-paneled bank office, a second-generation farmer reviews variable-rate mortgage documents to buy the neighbor's 300 acres, trading generational peace of mind for shiny green machinery and unpayable compound interest.
tracks.clean_lyrics:
The banker poured the coffee and he slid the page across
He said "A man who doesn't borrow is a man who accepts a loss"
He tapped his golden pen upon the line where I should sign
He said "Your land has doubled value since 1979"
I looked out at the parking lot, my truck was old and red
But on this piece of paper, I was rich, is what he said.

Leverage!
Borrow from the south to buy the north
Leverage!
Borrow from the third to pay the fourth
They aren't making any more of it, that's what the wise men say
So I'm betting on the heavy clay
Yeah, I'm betting on the heavy clay!

I bought the Miller place, I bought the section down the road
I didn't have the money but I took on all the load
It felt like winning poker when you haven't seen the cards
I was driving past my neighbors, tearing down their yards
It’s a magic kind of money, it’s a number in a book
It feels just like a handshake
(But it acts just like a hook)

Leverage!
Borrow from the south to buy the north
Leverage!
Borrow from the third to pay the fourth
They aren't making any more of it, that's what the wise men say
So I'm betting on the heavy clay
Yeah, I'm betting on the heavy clay!

At night I lie awake and I can hear the interest grow
It sounds like termites chewing in the basement down below
It eats while I am sleeping
It eats while I am awake
It’s the only thing on this whole farm that simply will not break.

Leverage!
Borrow from the south to buy the north
Leverage!
Borrow from the third to pay the fourth
They aren't making any more of it, that's what the wise men say
So I'm betting on the heavy clay
I'm betting on the heavy clay!

Just sign the line...
It never goes down...
Just sign the line...

tracks.title: The Crash of '80 (Interest Rates Rising)
tracks.vocal_profile: Haunting, strained Delta blues lead capturing tragic financial betrayal
tracks.theory: In October 1979, Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker hiked prime interest rates to 21.5% to curb urban stagflation, while President Carter enacted the 1980 Soviet grain embargo. Farmland values plummeted 60%, instantly wiping out farmer collateral and initiating the 1980s Farm Crisis.
tracks.summary: The devastating centerpiece of Act I. A stark, chilling account of watching the kitchen radio deliver interest rate announcements that turn solvent, hardworking families into debtors facing foreclosure by dawn.
tracks.clean_lyrics:
The radio said "Volcker" and the radio said "Change"
But the radio didn't mention the silence on the range
The man in the tall building, with the cigar and the frown
He decided that the inflation had to be put down
He didn't hold a shovel, he didn't hold a plow
But he reached across the country and he killed the dairy cow.

Eighteen percent!
The number on the wall.
Eighteen percent!
Watch the kingdom fall.
The corn is in the cradle but the note is coming due
And the money that I borrowed is eating me and you
It’s a drought of paper, it’s a flood of red
Eighteen percent is heavy as lead.

Then Carter closed the borders to the Russian hungry mouths
And the price of bushels plummeted all across the south
We did just what they told us, we planted fence to fence
But now the market's broken and it doesn't make no sense
The bin is full of harvest that no one wants to buy
And the banker stopped the coffee and he won't look in my eye.

Eighteen percent!
The number on the wall.
Eighteen percent!
Watch the kingdom fall.
The corn is in the cradle but the note is coming due
And the money that I borrowed is eating me and you
It’s a drought of paper, it’s a flood of red
Eighteen percent is heavy as lead.

I walked out to the mailbox.
I saw the yellow letter.
Foreclosure.
It’s a fancy word for stealing.
It’s a fancy word for death.
The math changed.
The rules changed.
But the debt... the debt stayed exactly the same.

Eighteen percent!
The number on the wall.
Eighteen percent!
Watch the kingdom fall.
It’s a drought of paper, it’s a flood of red
Eighteen percent is heavy as lead.

Heavy as lead...
The math changed...
Heavy as lead...

tracks.title: The Big Four
tracks.vocal_profile: Cynical, spoken-sung industrial blues lead trading lines with heavy distortion
tracks.theory: Four multinational conglomerates (Tyson, JBS, Cargill, National Beef) control over 85% of steer slaughter in the United States. This structural monopsony enables packers to suppress livestock purchase prices via captive supplies while simultaneously price-gouging retail consumers.
tracks.summary: A cattle rancher stares down a multi-lane concrete feedlot alley, realizing that four corporations hold the keys to every gate in the country, dictating auction prices with take-it-or-leave-it formula contracts.
tracks.clean_lyrics:
There's a million miles of barbed wire fence
There's a million hungry mouths to feed
But the road between the pasture and the plate
Is controlled by a special breed
They don't raise the calf, they don't grow the hay
They don't watch the sky for rain
They just stand in the middle of the narrow gate
And they collect the golden grain.

Four pairs of hands hold the bottleneck
Four kings sitting on a stacked deck
You pay twenty at the store, I get pennies on the pound
While the Big Four spin the whole world round
It’s an hourglass economy, can’t you see?
They’re squeezing you and they’re crushing me.

Walk down the aisle at the grocery store
You see a hundred brands on the shelf
It looks like freedom, it looks like choice
But you’re only fooling yourself
Different stickers, different names, different colored wrap
But it all flows back to the same four laps
They own the truck, they own the plant, they own the government hall
And the man who feeds the steer gets nothing at all.

Four pairs of hands hold the bottleneck
Four kings sitting on a stacked deck
You pay twenty at the store, I get pennies on the pound
While the Big Four spin the whole world round
It’s an hourglass economy, can’t you see?
They’re squeezing you and they’re crushing me.

Tyson.
Cargill.
JBS.
National Beef.
Eighty-five percent of the market.
Eighty-five percent of the blood.
We are just the raw material.
You are just the wallet.
And they are the knife.

Four pairs of hands hold the bottleneck
Four kings sitting on a stacked deck
You pay twenty at the store, I get pennies on the pound
While the Big Four spin the whole world round
It’s an hourglass economy, can’t you see?
They’re squeezing you and they’re crushing me.

Squeezing you...
Crushing me...
The bottleneck...

tracks.title: 14 Cents (The Grocer's Lie)
tracks.tagline: The Breakdown of the Food Dollar
tracks.vocal_profile: Fast, rhythmic country talking blues with razor-sharp satirical cadence
tracks.theory: According to USDA Economic Research Service data, the farmer's share of the consumer food dollar has collapsed from 41 cents in 1950 and 31 cents in 1980 to a meager 14.3 cents today. The remaining 85.7 cents is captured by processors, packaging, advertising, and retail distribution.
tracks.summary: A fast-paced, razor-sharp talking blues breaking down the absurd economic ledger of supermarket shelves, where the plastic wrapper, barcode scan, and shelf placement earn ten times more than the farmer who plowed the dirt.
tracks.clean_lyrics:
Let's do the math.
Take a dollar out of your pocket.
Lay it on the table.
Now watch it disappear.

You bought a box of cereal for six ninety-nine
You think I’m driving Cadillacs and drinking fine wine
You see the picture on the box, the barn and the sun
You think the farmer’s victory has finally been won
But strip away the plastic and strip away the glue
Strip away the trucking and the advertising crew
Strip away the CEO who needs a brand new jet
And take a look at what the man in overalls will get.

Fourteen cents!
That’s the slice of the pie.
Fourteen cents!
Don’t believe the grocer’s lie.
The box cost a nickel, the ad cost a dime
The shelf space cost a quarter, it’s a capital crime
You’re paying for the logo, you’re paying for the shine
But for the wheat inside the box?
I get fourteen cents of every dollar on the line.

They tell you that the supply chain is broken and loose
They tell you that the fuel cost is giving them the excuse
But look at the earnings call, look at the quarterly sheet
They’re making record profits while you can’t afford to eat
I grew the corn for the flakes, I grew the wheat for the bread
But the middleman is fat and the farmer’s in the red.
If I gave you the wheat for free, gave it as a gift
The price of that box wouldn't hardly even shift.

Fourteen cents!
That’s the slice of the pie.
Fourteen cents!
Don’t believe the grocer’s lie.
The box cost a nickel, the ad cost a dime
The shelf space cost a quarter, it’s a capital crime
You’re paying for the logo, you’re paying for the shine
But for the wheat inside the box?
I get fourteen cents of every dollar on the line.

Processing.
Packaging.
Transportation.
Wholesaling.
Retailing.
Marketing.
Farming.
We are the last ones to get paid.
And we are the first ones to go broke.

Fourteen cents!
That’s the slice of the pie.
Fourteen cents!
Don’t believe the grocer’s lie.
You’re paying for the logo, you’re paying for the shine
But for the wheat inside the box?
I get fourteen cents of every dollar on the line.

Keep your change...
Fourteen cents...
The rest is just air...

tracks.title: Soybeans in the Silo (The Trade War Blues)
tracks.tagline: Tariff Casualties & The Ghost Fleet of Grain
tracks.vocal_profile: Slow, heavy acoustic bottleneck blues lead with deep resonance
tracks.theory: Family farmers bear the immediate brunt of international trade disputes and retaliatory tariffs. When retaliatory tariffs closed Pacific export ports, millions of bushels of soybeans spoiled in auxiliary grain bags and silos while emergency federal bailout payments masked structural collapse.
tracks.summary: A slow, resonant bottleneck blues set against the silhouette of towering corrugated steel silos overflowing with unexportable grain, exposing how small growers are used as expendable poker chips in geopolitical negotiations.
tracks.clean_lyrics:
The combine ran perfect, the rain came on time
The pods were all bursting, the yield was prime
We cut until midnight, we filled up the trucks
We thought we had finally changed our luck
But when we got to the river, the gates were all barred
And the man at the scale looked weary and hard
He said "Don't dump it here, son, the barges won't load
Turn that rig around and go back down the road."

Soybeans in the silo, rotting in the heat
A mountain of gold that we can't afford to eat
Washington is gambling, playing poker with the Xi
But the chips on the table are my family and me
The ships are all anchored, the ocean is wide
And we're drowning right here in a yellow harvest tide.

They said "Hold on a minute, it's just for a while"
They said "Take the payment and force out a smile"
But a market once lost is a hard thing to find
Like a lover you left in a bad frame of mind
Now the boats go to Santos, down in Brazil
They're cutting the rainforest just to fill up the bill
We lost the customer while we fought the war
And they ain't coming back to this dock anymore.

Soybeans in the silo, rotting in the heat
A mountain of gold that we can't afford to eat
Washington is gambling, playing poker with the Xi
But the chips on the table are my family and me
The ships are all anchored, the ocean is wide
And we're drowning right here in a yellow harvest tide.

You can store it in a bag.
You can pile it on the ground.
But you can't pay the bank with a pile on a mound.
It's just gravity now.
Heavy.
Useless.
Weight.

Soybeans in the silo, rotting in the heat
A mountain of gold that we can't afford to eat
The ships are all anchored, the ocean is wide
And we're drowning right here in a yellow harvest tide.

Rotting in the heat...
Down in Brazil...
Just gravity now...

tracks.title: The Tournament (A Poultry Affair)
tracks.tagline: Indentured Labor & The Relative Ranking System
tracks.vocal_profile: Claustrophobic, high-tension Southern rock baritone with frantic urgency
tracks.theory: In contract poultry farming, integrators force independent growers into a zero-sum 'tournament system.' Farmers carry 100% of the capital debt for chicken houses while integrators control the chicks, feed quality, and medicine, pitting neighbor against neighbor in a rigged compensation ranking.
tracks.summary: Act III opens in the suffocating heat of a 20,000-bird poultry barn at 2 AM, documenting the psychological desperation of a contract grower trapped under massive bank debt while corporate integrators dock pay on rigged feed-conversion metrics.
tracks.clean_lyrics:
The truck comes at midnight, the lights cut the dark
They drop off the chicks like animals onto an ark
Thirty thousand souls in a tunnel of tin
That’s where the worry and the sweating begin
The birds are the Company's, the feed is their loan
The debt and the dead ones are mine all alone
I walk through the house with a bucket and pail
Checking the water and watching the scale.

It’s a tournament, boys, on the settlement sheet
I’m fighting my neighbor for the price of the meat
If I climb the ladder, then Billy must fall
There isn't enough money to cover us all
They grade on a curve, they grade on the spread
I need you to fail so I can get fed
Yeah, I need you to fail so I can get fed.

I saw the feed truck pull up to Miller’s last week
It looked like the high-protein, polished and sleek
But the load that they dumped in my hopper today
Looked dusty and dry, like ground-up old hay
Did I make the wrong angry call to the boss?
Did they mark down my name for a calculated loss?
You can't trust the inputs, you can't trust the game
When the variables change but the pay is the same.

It’s a tournament, boys, on the settlement sheet
I’m fighting my neighbor for the price of the meat
If I climb the ladder, then Billy must fall
There isn't enough money to cover us all
They grade on a curve, they grade on the spread
I need you to fail so I can get fed
Yeah, I need you to fail so I can get fed.

Six weeks.
Get 'em fat.
Get 'em out.
Wait for the envelope.
Am I Number One?
Or am I Number Ten?
If I'm Number One, I buy groceries.
If I'm Number Ten, I sell the truck.
Sorry, Billy.
It’s just business.

It’s a tournament, boys, on the settlement sheet
I’m fighting my neighbor for the price of the meat
If I climb the ladder, then Billy must fall
There isn't enough money to cover us all
They grade on a curve, they grade on the spread
I need you to fail so I can get fed.

I need you to fail...
Sorry Billy...
Watch the scale...

tracks.title: The Technology Fee (Sterile Seeds)
tracks.tagline: Patented Germplasm & The Criminalization of Seed Saving
tracks.vocal_profile: Grim, mechanical acoustic blues lead contrasting biological wonder and corporate lock
tracks.theory: The 1980 Supreme Court decision Diamond v. Chakrabarty and subsequent plant patent rulings permitted utility patents on living organism genomes. Seed prices jumped over 700% as agrochemical giants bundled patented herbicide-tolerant seeds with mandatory annual technology user fees.
tracks.summary: Contrasting a grandfather's sacred Mason jar of saved heirloom seed with contemporary corporate seed bags accompanied by 40-page binding legal licenses and private investigator surveillance teams.
tracks.clean_lyrics:
My granddaddy kept a jar above the kitchen sink
Filled with the heavy kernels, black and purple link
He’d walk the rows in August and find the strongest stalk
He’d save the future harvest with a quiet little walk
It was a circle unbroken, a gift from year to year
But now the jar is empty and the patent man is here.

Pay the fee.
Sign the line.
What grows in the dirt isn't yours or mine.
It’s Intellectual Property, it’s a coded gene
It’s software for the soil, it’s a part of the machine.
Don't you dare save a seed, don't you dare try to cheat
You have to rent the life inside the winter wheat.

I went down to the dealer to buy the spring supply
He handed me a contract with a cold and steady eye
"Technology Stewardship," that's what the paper said
It means I own the labor but they own the bread
If the wind blows the pollen across the county line
And lands upon a neighbor who didn't pay the fine
The lawyers come in black cars to test the DNA
And take the farm away before the light of day.

Pay the fee.
Sign the line.
What grows in the dirt isn't yours or mine.
It’s Intellectual Property, it’s a coded gene
It’s software for the soil, it’s a part of the machine.
Don't you dare save a seed, don't you dare try to cheat
You have to rent the life inside the winter wheat.

Roundup Ready.
Liberty Link.
Terminator.
They designed it to die.
It grows once.
And then it quits.
Just like a lightbulb.
Just like us.

Pay the fee.
Sign the line.
What grows in the dirt isn't yours or mine.
It’s Intellectual Property, it’s a coded gene
It’s software for the soil, it’s a part of the machine.
You have to rent the life inside the winter wheat.

Rent the life...
Pay the fee...
One time use...

tracks.title: Code 502 (The Digital Leash)
tracks.tagline: DRM Lockouts & The Right to Repair
tracks.vocal_profile: Aggressive, percussive folk-rock vocal delivered through overdriven vintage mic
tracks.theory: Modern agricultural equipment uses encrypted CAN-bus digital locks and proprietary firmware. Under Section 1201 of the DMCA, manufacturers lock out independent farmers and mechanics from calibrating minor sensors, requiring $180/hr dealer technicians with encrypted software keys.
tracks.summary: Rain clouds gather on the western horizon while a half-million-dollar combine sits motionless in the mud because a faulty $15 exhaust sensor threw an un-resettable 'Code 502' software error that only a distant corporate technician is legally allowed to clear.
tracks.clean_lyrics:
The clouds are turning purple in the western sky
The beans are dry and ready and the yield is high
I’m running down the rows trying to beat the rain
When suddenly the dashboard screams in digital pain
The engine cuts the power, the hydraulics die
I’m sitting in a dead machine and wondering why
I open up the panel with a greasy hand
But the trouble isn't metal, it’s a software command.

Code Five-Oh-Two!
The screen is blinking red.
Code Five-Oh-Two!
The tractor is dead.
I got a toolbox full of wrenches, I got a lifetime of skill
But I can't fix a sensor that is programmed to kill
It’s a digital leash, it’s a corporate lock
I’m stranded in the field while they watch the clock.

I called the dealer up, I said "I need a fix"
He said "I can't get a tech out here until day number six"
I said "I know what's broken, just give me the key"
He said "I can't let you touch it, that’s piracy"
Piracy? I paid half a million for this steel!
But I don't own the brain, I only own the wheel
So the rain is coming down and the crop is going to rot
Because a lawyer in the city tied a digital knot.

Code Five-Oh-Two!
The screen is blinking red.
Code Five-Oh-Two!
The tractor is dead.
I got a toolbox full of wrenches, I got a lifetime of skill
But I can't fix a sensor that is programmed to kill
It’s a digital leash, it’s a corporate lock
I’m stranded in the field while they watch the clock.

John Deere.
Case IH.
New Holland.
They put a padlock on the engine.
They put a tollbooth in the cab.
I used to be a mechanic.
Now I'm just a user.
Error!

Code Five-Oh-Two!
The screen is blinking red.
Code Five-Oh-Two!
The tractor is dead.
It’s a digital leash, it’s a corporate lock
I’m stranded in the field while they watch the clock.

Code Five-Oh-Two...
System Failure...
Contact Administrator...

tracks.title: Drift (The Neighbor's War)
tracks.vocal_profile: Brooding, mournful Southern Gothic baritone over weeping slide guitar
tracks.theory: The introduction of volatile synthetic auxins like Dicamba sparked widespread agricultural litigation. When sprayed on GMO-tolerant crops, the chemical volatilizes and drifts for miles, destroying non-tolerant crops, specialty orchards, and organic farms—forcing growers to buy defensive patented seed.
tracks.summary: Act IV delves into the tragic fracture of rural social fabric. Longtime neighbors and church elders are pitted against one another in bitter lawsuits after drifting chemical clouds curl and burn peach trees and non-GMO vegetable crops.
tracks.clean_lyrics:
The heat was heavy on the first of July
Not a single cloud in the burning sky
I saw the sprayer moving on the ridge to the west
Billy was trying to put the weeds to rest
He followed the label, or so he claimed
But the wind is a creature that cannot be tamed
It picked up the vapor like a ghost in the air
And it carried the poison with a devil's care.

Drift.
It crosses the fence line, invisible and silent.
Drift.
A chemical war that is quiet and violent.
Now the leaves are cupping like a begging hand
Twisted and scarred all across the land
The wind used to bring us the rain and the seed
Now it just brings us the greed.
Drift.

I walked the rows on a Tuesday morn
And I saw the sign that the leaves were torn
Curled up tight in a chemical burn
The sickening twisted and yellow turn
I drove to the diner but Billy wasn't there
Or maybe he saw me and went elsewhere
We used to trade labor, we used to trade tools
Now we talk through the lawyers and follow the rules.

Drift.
It crosses the fence line, invisible and silent.
Drift.
A chemical war that is quiet and violent.
Now the leaves are cupping like a begging hand
Twisted and scarred all across the land
The wind used to bring us the rain and the seed
Now it just brings us the greed.
Drift.

They sold him a seed that could take the spray.
They sold me a seed that stood in the way.
They made the poison.
They made the cure.
And they made sure that neither of us feels secure.
Now I'm suing Billy.
And Billy's suing me.
And the company is laughing all the way to the sea.

Drift.
It crosses the fence line, invisible and silent.
Drift.
A chemical war that is quiet and violent.
Now the leaves are cupping like a begging hand
Twisted and scarred all across the land.
Drift.

Like a begging hand...
Crosses the line...
The wind...

tracks.title: The Auctioneer’s Dirge (Sold by the Pound)
tracks.tagline: The Foreclosure Gavel & The Liquidation of Heritage
tracks.vocal_profile: Rapid-fire auction chant cadence alternating with slow, tragic funeral chorus
tracks.theory: Foreclosure auctions represent the terminal symptom of agrarian debt deflations. Family heirlooms, work tools, livestock, and hundred-year-old homesteads are liquidated under the sheriff's gavel, usually purchased for pennies on the dollar by institutional land investment trusts.
tracks.summary: A chilling juxtaposition of the fast-talking auction chant with slow, sorrowful funeral choir chords, capturing the day four generations of sweat, hand-turned wrenches, and family soil are sold off in lot numbers under a gray autumn drizzle.
tracks.clean_lyrics:
Ladies and gentlemen.
Terms are cash.
Everything must go.

Alright who will give me ten
Who will give me ten dollars
I got ten now twenty
Will you give me twenty dollars
Looking for a twenty
I see twenty in the back
Now thirty
Thirty on the rake
Thirty on the rust
Who will give me forty
For the memories and dust
I got thirty looking forty
Will you give me forty five
Selling off the legacy
While the man is still alive.

Going once...
The history of the hand.
Going twice...
The spirit of the land.
Sold!
To the stranger in the truck.
Sold!
For a dollar and some luck.

Now look at this tractor
John Deere four zero two zero
Run a little rough but she is a hero
Who will give me five thousand
Five thousand on the green
Best hydraulics that you have ever seen
I got five now six
Will you give me six
Don't look at the family
Just look at the fix
I got six thousand dollars
Do I hear a seven
Selling off the earth
And hoping for a heaven.

Going once...
The history of the hand.
Going twice...
The spirit of the land.
Sold!
To the stranger in the truck.
Sold!
For a dollar and some luck.

The neighbors are watching.
They are buying the tools.
They are buying the wrenches.
They won't look me in the eye.
Because they know.
Next week.
It might be them.

Alright last call
Last call on the lot
Selling everything we have
Selling everything we got
Who will give me one dollar
Who will give me one
For the kitchen table
And the setting sun
One dollar
Two dollars
Sold to the bank.

Sold.

tracks.title: Empty Main Street (The Hollowing Out)
tracks.tagline: Rural Decay & The Export of the Next Generation
tracks.vocal_profile: Eerie, spacious ghost-town folk vocal echoing across deserted streets
tracks.theory: Farm consolidation eliminates the rural customer base that sustains local commerce. As family farms are consolidated into corporate mega-holdings, local grain elevators, hardware stores, schools, and hospitals close, leading to extreme rural brain drain and out-migration.
tracks.summary: Walking down the center line of a crumbling Midwestern county seat at noon on a Tuesday. The hardware store windows are covered in faded paper, the big-box store on the highway extracts wealth, and the community's greatest export is its children.
tracks.clean_lyrics:
I walked down the center line at noon on a Tuesday
Didn't see a car, didn't see a soul, didn't see a stray
The hardware store has paper on the glass since ninety-nine
The dust is getting thicker on the Welcome Rotary sign
The brick is turning crumble and the wood is turning grey
The money took the highway and it drove the other way.

It’s the hollowing out.
It’s the quiet decay.
The export of the dollar and the export of the hay.
The school is on the bus route, an hour down the road
The bank is just a website, a zip code and a node
Main Street is a ghost, a skeleton of pride
With nothing left but memories alive inside.

Out on the bypass, shining in the dark
There’s a bright yellow box with a concrete park
They sell the plastic buckets and the sugar and the trash
Extracting every penny of the local widow's cash
It killed the mom and pop, it killed the grocery store
A parasite of commerce knocking on the door.

It’s the hollowing out.
It’s the quiet decay.
The export of the dollar and the export of the hay.
The school is on the bus route, an hour down the road
The bank is just a website, a zip code and a node
Main Street is a ghost, a skeleton of pride
With nothing left but memories alive inside.

We export the corn.
We export the cattle.
We export the money.
But the saddest thing of all?
We export the children.
Because there is nothing here for them to do.
But leave.

It’s the hollowing out.
It’s the quiet decay.
Main Street is a ghost, a skeleton of pride
With nothing left but memories alive inside.

Just memories...
The Yellow Box...
Hollowing out...

tracks.title: The Valley of Death (Crossing Over)
tracks.tagline: The Multi-Year Agony of Biological Transition
tracks.vocal_profile: Intimate, determined Americana lead building into hopeful choral lift
tracks.theory: The 3-to-5 year transition from chemical-dependent agriculture to regenerative soil biological health is known as the 'Valley of Death.' Synthetic yields collapse before beneficial microbes, fungi, and natural soil nitrogen cycles are restored, creating immense short-term financial peril.
tracks.summary: Act V begins the arduous journey of healing. A farmer weans the soil off synthetic inputs, enduring the mocking stares of neighbors and nervous bank managers during year two, until the first wild earthworms and natural crumb structure return to the soil.
tracks.clean_lyrics:
I cut the anhydrous, I parked the big spray rig
The neighbors stopped waving, the mystery is big
They say "Look at his corn, it’s yellow and it’s small"
They say "By October, he won't have nothing at all"
The banker called on Friday, he asked about the plan
He said "You can't grow a profit without a chemical hand"
But I’m tired of the poison, I’m tired of the debt
I’m betting on a harvest that I haven't seen yet.

I’m walking through the Valley.
The Valley of Death.
The soil is in withdrawal, fighting for breath.
The yield is going down, the money is tight
But the worms are returning in the middle of the night.
It’s a three year journey across the burning sand
To get back to the promised land.

It’s an addiction, just like a needle in the vein
The dirt got so used to the synthetic rain
Now I took it away and the ground is in shock
I’m trading the quick fix for the solid rock
I dug a hole this morning, deep in the clay
And I saw a little life that wasn't there yesterday
A root going deep, a bug on the crawl
Maybe, just maybe, I won't lose it all.

I’m walking through the Valley.
The Valley of Death.
The soil is in withdrawal, fighting for breath.
The yield is going down, the money is tight
But the worms are returning in the middle of the night.
It’s a three year journey across the burning sand
To get back to the promised land.

Year one: The crash.
Year two: The struggle.
Year three: The waking up.
Hold on.
Just hold on.
The biology is slower than the chemistry.
But the biology lasts.

I’m walking through the Valley.
The Valley of Death.
The soil is in withdrawal, fighting for breath.
The yield is going down, the money is tight
But the worms are returning in the middle of the night.
It’s a three year journey across the burning sand
To get back to the promised land.

The worms are returning...
Hold on...
Year three...

tracks.title: Bust the Trust (Sherman's Ghost)
tracks.tagline: The Revival of Grassroots Antitrust Enforcement
tracks.vocal_profile: Defiant, driving roots-rock anthem vocal with fierce agrarian conviction
tracks.theory: The legal mechanism for agrarian restoration is the enforcement of the 1890 Sherman Antitrust Act, the 1914 Clayton Act, and the 1921 Packers and Stockyards Act. Restoring competitive, decentralized agricultural markets requires breaking up input monopolies and buyer cartels.
tracks.summary: A barn-burning roots-rock anthem invoking the spirit of John Sherman and the Populist prairie movements of the 1890s, calling on working people to break corporate strangleholds, unlock farm equipment, and reclaim the republic.
tracks.clean_lyrics:
Ready!

Old Teddy Roosevelt walked softly on the floor
But he carried a stick that could break down the door
He saw the railroads cheating and the oil tycoons
Eating up the country with their silver spoons
He said "Competition is the law of the land"
And he took the hammer from the tyrant's hand
But the ghost of the Gilded Age is back in town
And the Big Four meatpackers are doubling down.

Bust the Trust!
Break the chain!
Give the market back to the wind and the rain!
We don't want a handout, we don't want a check
We want the corporate boot off of our neck!
Sharpen the law, wipe off the rust
It’s time to stand up and Bust the Trust!

They tell us that big is efficient and cheap
But the price of the burger makes the mothers weep
While the rancher is selling the herd for a loss
Because four men in suits are the only boss
It isn't capitalism, it’s a rigged-up game
It’s a cartel hiding underneath a brand name
You can fix the soil, you can fix the gate
But you can't fix a market that is ruled by hate.

Bust the Trust!
Break the chain!
Give the market back to the wind and the rain!
We don't want a handout, we don't want a check
We want the corporate boot off of our neck!
Sharpen the law, wipe off the rust
It’s time to stand up and Bust the Trust!

The Sherman Act.
The Packers and Stockyards Act.
The laws are on the books.
They are just collecting dust.
While the monopolies collect the gold.
Blow the dust off.
Pick up the stick.
Pick up the stick!

Bust the Trust!
Break the chain!
Give the market back to the wind and the rain!
We don't want a handout, we don't want a check
We want the corporate boot off of our neck!
Sharpen the law, wipe off the rust
It’s time to stand up and Bust the Trust!

Bust the Trust!
Break them up!
Sherman's Ghost is walking...

tracks.title: The Farmer’s Broken Back (Anthem)
tracks.tagline: The Resilience of the Land & The Enduring Spine
tracks.vocal_profile: Soulful, soaring acoustic anthem building to a triumphant full-band climax
tracks.theory: Agrarian parity is not charity—it is the foundational prerequisite for ecological stewardship, democratic liberty, and cultural permanence. When the farmer stands upright, the entire social order finds its equilibrium on living soil.
tracks.summary: The monumental finale of the album. The broken back of the farmer becomes both an indictment of systemic corporate exploitation and a symbol of unbreakable resilience: corporations and empires fall, but the stewards of the soil will remain.
tracks.clean_lyrics:
I carry the weight of the Earl Butz lie
I carry the debt underneath the sky
I planted the fencerows and tore down the trees
I spent fifty years on my bended knees
My spine is twisted like an old barbed wire
From hauling the water and fighting the fire
The doctor says "Son, you have worn out the frame"
I said "Doc, the whole country has done just the same."

They broke the bank.
They broke the plow.
They broke the market and the dairy cow.
They rigged the game with a unseen stack
But they built this nation on the farmer's broken back.
Yeah, the food on the table and the shirt on the rack
Is holding up the world on a farmer's broken back.

We survived the crash of nineteen-eighty-one
We survived the scorching of the trade war sun
We fought the tournament and we fought the rust
We watched the main street turn into dust
They treat us like gears in a big machine
Just a data point on a digital screen
But a gear doesn't bleed and a gear doesn't pray
And a gear doesn't wake up to greet the day.

They broke the bank.
They broke the plow.
They broke the market and the dairy cow.
They rigged the game with a unseen stack
But they built this nation on the farmer's broken back.
Yeah, the food on the table and the shirt on the rack

If we stop the tractor, the city goes dark.

You can patent the seed, you can steal the yield.
But you can't take the soul from the middle of the field.
We are bent.
But we are not broken.

Yeah, we're holding up the world on a farmer's broken back!

We're still here.
Just look at the field.
We're still here.

exhibits.title: The Expansion Trap & The 1980s Interest Spike
exhibits.body_1: In 1973, USDA Secretary Earl Butz urged American farmers to plant 'fencerow to fencerow' to feed export demand from the Soviet Union. Guaranteed land appreciation and bank cheerleading drove unprecedented debt accumulation. But in 1979, the Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker hiked prime interest rates to 21.5% to curb inflation, while President Carter imposed a Soviet grain embargo in 1980.
exhibits.body_2: Land values plummeted by more than 60% across the Corn Belt overnight. Farmers who held 80% equity on paper saw their collateral vanish while variable-rate debt skyrocketed. The resulting tidal wave of foreclosures precipitated the deepest rural crisis since the Great Depression and altered the demographic fabric of the heartland forever.

exhibits.title: The 14.3¢ Food Dollar & The Big Four Meatpackers
exhibits.stat_1_lbl: Current Farm Share of Food Dollar
exhibits.body_1: According to the USDA Economic Research Service, the farmer's share of the retail consumer food dollar has steadily eroded from over 50 cents in the 1950s to just 14.3 cents today. The remaining 85.7 cents is captured by processors, packaging conglomerates, transportation logistics, distributors, and mega-retailers.
exhibits.body_2: In beef packing, just four multinational corporations (Tyson, JBS, Cargill, and National Beef) control over 85% of steer and heifer slaughter. This extreme market concentration creates a captive buyer bottleneck: ranchers and feedlots have no alternative buyers, forcing them to accept predatory grid-pricing formulas while supermarket meat prices soar.

exhibits.title: The Digital Leash & Sterile Seed Patents
exhibits.body_1: The shift from traditional capital equipment to corporate-controlled technological enclosures has redefined property rights on the farm. Modern tractors, combines, and sprayers are equipped with digital rights management (DRM) and Controller Area Network (CAN) bus encryption that lock farmers out of independent diagnostic repairs. When an arbitrary 'Code 502' sensor error triggers during harvest, the machine halts until a certified dealer travels out with proprietary software keys.
exhibits.body_2: Simultaneously, seed patents on genetically modified traits prohibit the ancient practice of seed saving. Farmers purchase one-time usage licenses alongside mandatory chemical packages, subject to private corporate investigators and patent infringement litigation.

exhibits.title: Bust the Trust & Agrarian Parity Restoration
exhibits.body_1: True agrarian renewal does not lie in emergency corporate bailout checks, but in systemic antitrust enforcement, supply-demand management, and mandatory market transparency. Drawing on the legacy of the 1890 Sherman Antitrust Act, the 1921 Packers and Stockyards Act, and the original 1933 Agricultural Adjustment Act, family farm advocates demand the revival of agricultural parity.
exhibits.body_2: Key policy remediation includes breaking up meatpacking and seed monopolies, passing federal Right to Repair legislation for all farm equipment, banning predatory tournament systems in contract poultry production, and establishing national strategic grain reserves that decouple farm livelihood from Wall Street commodity speculation.
